claim: Oscillations are generated by large neuronal ensembles and are a hallmark of the mammalian brain.
source: Oscillations, generated by large neuronal ensembles, are a hallmark of the mammalian brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004

claim: Oscillations are well preserved during evolution.
source: They are well preserved during evolution (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004

claim: Oscillations have been suggested to play a key role in high cognitive functions.
source: and have been suggested to play a key role in high cognitive functions (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010

claim: Oscillations enable the synchronization of neural activity within and across brain regions.
source: They enable the synchronization of neural activity within and across brain regions, thus promoting the precise temporal coordination of neural processes underlying memory, perception, and behavior (Colgin and Moser, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Colgin and Moser, 2010

claim: Disruption of oscillations leads to cognitive and sensorimotor deficits associated with several neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Their disruption leads to cognitive and sensorimotor deficits associated with several neuropsychiatric diseases (Uhlhaas et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uhlhaas et al., 2011

claim: Oscillations occurring at different frequency bands (from 0.5 to 200 Hz) interact with each other through hierarchical cross-frequency coupling.
source: Oscillations occurring at different frequency bands (from 0.5 to 200 Hz), interact with each other through hierarchical cross-frequency coupling (González et al., 2020; Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Tort et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to González et al., 2020; Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Tort et al., 2008

claim: Cross-frequency interactions are linked to different computational operations or different phases in a computational operation.
source: Such interactions are linked to different computational operations or different phases in a computational operation and are thought to characterize distinct brain states supporting various aspects of behavior (McCormick et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCormick et al., 2020

claim: In the hippocampus, theta cycles are often nested with bouts of faster oscillations in the gamma frequency.
source: In the hippocampus, theta cycles are often nested with bouts of faster oscillations in the gamma frequency and are thought to be related to different stages of memory processing (Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lopes-Dos-Santos et al., 2018

claim: During wakefulness, the CA1 region is characterized by cross-frequency coupling between theta and distinct gamma oscillations.
source: Specifically, during wakefulness, the CA1 region is characterized by cross-frequency coupling between theta and distinct gamma oscillations, which exhibit their peak power at distinct phases of ongoing slow oscillations (Belluscio et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Colgin et al., 2009; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Scheffer-Teixeira et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Belluscio et al., 2012; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Colgin et al., 2009; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Scheffer-Teixeira et al., 2012; Yamamoto et al., 2014

claim: The slow, medium, and fast gamma oscillations emerge from stratum radiatum (SR), stratum lacunosum moleculare (SLM), and stratum pyramidale (SP), respectively.
source: The slow, medium, and fast gamma oscillations, emerging from stratum radiatum (SR), stratum lacunosum moleculare (SLM), and stratum pyramidale (SP), respectively, are linked to network activity in entorhinal cortex, CA3 and CA1 region, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Guardamagna et al., 2023; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Schomburg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colgin et al., 2009; Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2017; Guardamagna et al., 2023; Lasztóczi and Klausberger, 2016; Schomburg et al., 2014

claim: During sleep, theta and medium gamma oscillations dominate the rapid eye movement REM sleep.
source: During sleep, theta and medium gamma oscillations dominate the rapid eye movement REM sleep, whereas delta, beta frequency band, and ripples or fast gamma (100–200 Hz), linked to memory consolidation processes, dominate the non-REM sleep (Battaglia et al., 2011; Buzsáki, 1989; Genzel et al., 2014; Roumis and Frank, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Battaglia et al., 2011; Buzsáki, 1989; Genzel et al., 2014; Roumis and Frank, 2015

claim: Delta, beta frequency band, and ripples or fast gamma (100–200 Hz) dominate the non-REM sleep and are linked to memory consolidation processes.
source: During sleep, theta and medium gamma oscillations dominate the rapid eye movement REM sleep, whereas delta, beta frequency band, and ripples or fast gamma (100–200 Hz), linked to memory consolidation processes, dominate the non-REM sleep (Battaglia et al., 2011; Buzsáki, 1989; Genzel et al., 2014; Roumis and Frank, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Battaglia et al., 2011; Buzsáki, 1989; Genzel et al., 2014; Roumis and Frank, 2015

claim: Oscillations are known to modulate the firing activity of individual cells.
source: Oscillations are generated by neuronal population, and they in turn are known to modulate the firing activity of individual cells (Benchenane et al., 2010; Hulse et al., 2017; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benchenane et al., 2010; Hulse et al., 2017; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993

claim: Neuronal firing has been classically characterized in the context of a single-frequency band during distinct brain states.
source: Classically, neuronal firing has been characterized in the context of a single-frequency band during distinct brain states (Fox et al., 1986; Henze et al., 2000; Hafting et al., 2008; van Wingerden et al., 2010; Siapas et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fox et al., 1986; Henze et al., 2000; Hafting et al., 2008; van Wingerden et al., 2010; Siapas et al., 2005

claim: Four male C57BL/6J mice were used in the study.
source: Four male C57BL/6J mice (Charles River) were used in this study, all implanted with a Hybrid Drive.
evidence: Direct statement in methods section

claim: Brain activity was recorded in freely moving mice during four consecutive trials: Sleep1, Novel Arena-1 Exploration, Novel Arena-2 Exploration, and Sleep2.
source: On a single day, we recorded brain activity in freely moving mice (n = 4) during four consecutive trials: (1) Sleep1, (2) Novel Arena-1 Exploration, (3) Novel Arena-2 Exploration, and (4) Sleep2, (Figure 1A).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1A

claim: Layer-resolved LFP were extracted from the CA1 region of the dorsal hippocampus using multisite silicon probes.
source: Layer-resolved LFP were extracted from the CA1 region of the dorsal hippocampus using multisite silicon probes (Figure 1B; Guardamagna et al., 2022).
evidence: Described in methods with reference to Figure 1B and citation to Guardamagna et al., 2022

claim: LFPs from SP, SR, and SLM layers were used to extract signals in six frequency bands: delta (1–5 Hz), theta (6–10 Hz), beta (10–20 Hz), slow gamma (20–45 Hz), medium gamma (60–90 Hz), and fast gamma (100–200 Hz).
source: LFPs from SP, SR, and SLM layers were used to extract signals in the following frequency bands: delta (1–5 Hz), theta (6–10 Hz), beta (10–20 Hz), slow gamma (20–45 Hz), medium gamma (60–90 Hz), and fast gamma (100–200 Hz).
evidence: Direct statement in methods section

claim: 18 frequency bands (six from each layer) were used to compute median power in nonoverlapping bins of 200 milliseconds.
source: Each of these 18 frequency bands (six from each layer, Figure 1C) were used to compute median power in nonoverlapping bins of 200 milliseconds and then smoothed using Gaussian kernel.
evidence: Described in methods with reference to Figure 1C

claim: UMAP was employed to reduce the dimensionality of the network state space from 18D to 2D.
source: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP, McInnes et al., 2020) was employed to reduce the dimensionality of the network state space from 18D to 2D (Figures 1C and 2A).
evidence: Described in methods with citation to McInnes et al., 2020 and reference to Figures 1C and 2A

claim: During awake trials the activity of the network was restricted to a subset of the states, whereas during sleep periods, it occupied a significantly larger area of the state space.
source: We observed that during awake trials the activity of the network was restricted to a subset of the states, whereas during sleep periods, it occupied a significantly larger area of the state space.
evidence: Observation from data analysis described in results

claim: The observed difference in occupancy between sleep and awake trials was significantly different from those computed in surrogate data.
source: We found that the observed difference in occupancy between sleep and awake trials was significantly different from those computed in surrogate data (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical comparison with surrogate data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The restricted occupancy during wakefulness is independent of trial duration.
source: We observed similar restrictions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the restricted occupancy during wakefulness is independent of trial duration.
evidence: Control analysis described in results with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Functional organization of network oscillations during sleep and wakefulness is conserved across species.
source: To further validate our findings, we computed the network state space and occupancy for the datasets recorded from freely moving rats in similar experimental conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and observed remarkable similarities in restrictions on the state space, suggesting that functional organization of network oscillations during sleep and wakefulness is conserved across species.
evidence: Comparison with rat data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: The network occupies the same set of states when animals explore distinct arenas.
source: In addition, we observed that the network occupies the same set of states when animals explore distinct arenas (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The restrictions on the state space are primarily dependent on the behavioral state of the animal rather than environmental factors.
source: Hence, the restrictions are primarily dependent on the behavioral state of the animal rather than environmental factors.
evidence: Inference from observation that network occupies same states in distinct arenas

claim: The restricted subspace of the state space occupied during wakefulness corresponds to states with low delta power, moderate beta power, and moderate to high gamma power.
source: For instance, the restricted subspace of the state space occupied during wakefulness corresponds to states with low delta power, moderate beta power, and moderate to high gamma power.
evidence: Observation from power overlay maps described in results

claim: During sleep, network oscillations exhibit broader range of operations since the power of each oscillation varies from its minima to its maxima.
source: However, during sleep, network oscillations exhibit broader range of operations since the power of each oscillation varies from its minima to its maxima as evident in the overlay maps (Figure 3A).
evidence: Observation from power overlay maps shown in Figure 3A

claim: REM states are characterized by moderate to high power in beta, slow, medium, and fast gamma oscillatory bands simultaneously with theta oscillations.
source: Visual inspection of power overlay maps (Figure 3A and REM and non-REM states localization maps in Figure 4A and B) revealed that REM states are characterized by moderate to high power in beta, slow, medium, and fast gamma oscillatory bands simultaneously with theta oscillations
evidence: Visual inspection of power overlay maps in Figures 3A, 4A, and 4B

claim: Non-REM states are characterized by the presence of moderate to high power in theta, slow, and fast gamma oscillations along with delta and beta.
source: whereas non-REM states are characterized by the presence of moderate to high power in theta, slow, and fast gamma oscillations along with delta and beta.
evidence: Visual inspection of power overlay maps described in results

claim: Medium gamma oscillations operate in low-power mode during non-REM sleep.
source: Notably, the medium gamma oscillations operate in low-power mode during non-REM sleep.
evidence: Observation from power overlay maps described in results

claim: The median density of awake trials (0.13 ± 0.009) was significantly higher than that detected during sleep (0.03 ± 0.0005).
source: Mirroring the smaller occupied state space region, the median density of awake trials was significantly higher than that detected during sleep (0.13 ± 0.009 versus 0.03 ± 0.0005).
evidence: Quantitative data from density analysis

claim: There was an increase in the median density of non-REM states during post-exploration sleep (Sleep2: 0.048 ± 0.002) compared to pre-exploration sleep (Sleep1: 0.039 ± 0.001).
source: We observed an increase in the median density of non-REM states during post-exploration sleep (Figure 4G: center; Sleep1: 0.039 ± 0.001versus Sleep2: 0.048 ± 0.002)
evidence: Quantitative data from density analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Changes in density of individual oscillations after learning have been reported and are thought to support memory consolidation.
source: In fact, changes in density of individual oscillations after learning have been reported using traditional analytical methods and are thought to support memory consolidation (Bakker et al., 2015; Eschenko et al., 2008; Eschenko et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bakker et al., 2015; Eschenko et al., 2008; Eschenko et al., 2006

claim: Distinct configuration of frequency band's correlations were observed during sleep and awake trails.
source: We observed distinct configuration of frequency band's correlations during sleep and awake trails (Figure 5B).
evidence: Observation from correlation matrix analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Distinct coupling configurations for awake, REM, and non-REM states were observed.
source: We employed UMAP to visualize the variability across correlation matrices. (Figure 5D) and observed distinct coupling configurations for awake, REM, and non-REM states (Figure 5E).
evidence: Observation from correlation matrix space analysis shown in Figures 5D and 5E

claim: During REM, there was increased coupling (positive correlation) among beta and slow gamma oscillations as well as among medium and fast gamma bands accompanied by decoupling (negative correlation) with delta.
source: During REM, we found increased coupling (positive correlation) among beta and slow gamma oscillations as well as among medium and fast gamma bands accompanied by decoupling (negative correlation) with delta.
evidence: Observation from correlation matrix analysis described in results

claim: During non-REM sleep all oscillations except delta were coupled.
source: This organization among oscillations was altered during non-REM sleep as all oscillations except delta were coupled.
evidence: Observation from correlation matrix analysis described in results

claim: The AACP value of real data was beyond the 95th percentile of the distribution of shuffled data.
source: We observed that the AACP value of real data was beyond the 95th percentile of the distribution of shuffled data (Figure 6D)
evidence: Statistical comparison with shuffled data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Transitions occurring from REM-to-REM sleep and non-REM-to-non-REM sleep (intra-state transitions) are more vulnerable to plasticity after exploration as compared to inter-state transitions.
source: We found that transitions occurring from REM-to-REM sleep and non-REM-to-non-REM sleep (intra-state transitions) are more vulnerable to plasticity after exploration as compared to inter-state transitions (such as non-REM to REM, REM-to-intermediate, etc.) (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Observation from state transition analysis shown in Figures 6E and 6F

claim: A reduction in median coverage speed was observed during awake compared to sleep trials.
source: We observed a reduction in median coverage speed during awake compared to sleep trials (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from coverage speed analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: A sharp dip in coverage speed was associated with state transition to REM sleep.
source: We observed a sharp dip in coverage speed associated with state transition to REM sleep (Figure 7F, S10A).
evidence: Observation from coverage speed analysis shown in Figure 7F

claim: During the transition to REM sleep the network stabilizes on state space.
source: This further suggests that during the transition to REM sleep the network stabilizes on state space.
evidence: Inference from observation of sharp dip in coverage speed during REM transition

claim: The transition to REM was associated with a significant reduction of power in beta frequency band and with an increase of medium and fast gamma power.
source: However, this transition was also associated with a significant reduction of power in beta frequency band and with an increase of medium and fast gamma power (Figure 7G).
evidence: Observation from power analysis during REM transition shown in Figure 7G

claim: Slow gamma remained mostly unchanged during the REM epoch, but showed a significant average increase in its power in a window preceding the onset of REM sleep.
source: While slow gamma remained mostly unchanged during the REM epoch, we measured a significant average increase in its power in a window preceding the onset of REM sleep and extending for few tens of seconds.
evidence: Observation from power analysis during REM transition described in results

claim: The result of slow gamma power increase preceding REM is consistent with previous reports of slow gamma power decreasing over the initial part of a REM epoch.
source: This result is consistent with previous reports of slow gamma power decreasing over the initial part of a REM epoch (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019

claim: Distinct activation signatures on state space correspond to distinct firing rate maps during exploration.
source: We hypothesized that distinct activation signatures on state space may correspond to distinct firing rate maps during exploration.
evidence: Hypothesis stated in results section

claim: There was distinction of sleep signatures for low firing cells in the arena compared to the high-firing ones.
source: We observed distinction of sleep signatures for low firing cells in the arena compared to the high-firing ones (Figure 8F; see also Figure 8—figure supplement 3 for interneurons and pyramidal cells).
evidence: Observation from signature space analysis shown in Figure 8F

claim: Sparse firing cells during exploration exhibit preferential firing to non-REM states and are simultaneously modulated by high power in delta, theta, beta oscillations, as well as moderate power in slow and fast gamma oscillations.
source: Specifically, we observed that sparse firing cells during exploration exhibit preferential firing to non-REM states (from Figures 4A, B, 8F) and are therefore simultaneously modulated by high power in delta, theta, beta oscillations, as well as moderate power in slow and fast gamma oscillations (from Figure 3A).
evidence: Observation from signature space analysis with reference to Figures 3A, 4A, 4B, and 8F

claim: High-firing cells during exploration are differently orchestrated by simultaneously occurring sleep oscillations compared to sparse firing cells.
source: However, the high-firing cells during exploration are differently orchestrated by simultaneously occurring sleep oscillations as evident in Figure 8F.
evidence: Observation from signature space analysis shown in Figure 8F

claim: Distinct functional cells in hippocampal CA1 are tuned to distinct set of network states and have distinct activation signatures during sleep trials.
source: Altogether, this suggests that distinct functional cells in hippocampal CA1 are tuned to distinct set of network states and have distinct activation signatures during sleep trials.
evidence: Inference from observations of distinct sleep signatures for different cell types

claim: Mice lacking NLG3 occupy state space associated with lower power of oscillations compared to wild-type mice.
source: Overlay maps of power of different oscillations on the state space suggest that mice lacking NLG3 occupy state space associated with lower power of oscillations (Figure 8—figure supplement 4D, top).
evidence: Observation from NLG3 KO analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4D

claim: Comparing power of individual bands reveals significant reduction in mean power of delta, theta, beta, medium, and fast gamma frequency bands in NLG3 KO mice.
source: Comparing power of individual bands reveals significant reduction in mean power of delta, theta, beta, medium, and fast gamma frequency bands.
evidence: Quantitative comparison described in results for NLG3 KO analysis

claim: Only slow gamma power was not significantly different between wild-type and NLG3 KO mice.
source: Only slow gamma power was not significant.
evidence: Statistical comparison described in results for NLG3 KO analysis

claim: No differences in correlation among various oscillatory processes were observed across genotypes (wild-type vs NLG3 KO).
source: We next computed correlation among various oscillatory processes (Figure 8—figure supplement 5A and B) and observed no differences across genotypes.
evidence: Observation from correlation analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 5A and B

claim: No difference in speed of coverage was observed across genotypes (wild-type vs NLG3 KO).
source: Lastly, we computed the speed of coverage and observed no difference across genotypes.
evidence: Observation from coverage speed analysis described in results

claim: NLG3 KO mice show altered co-occurrence patterns along with intact coupling and transition properties of hippocampal oscillations.
source: Altogether, this suggests altered co-occurrence patterns along with intact coupling and transition properties of hippocampal oscillations in NLG3 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: Summary of observations from NLG3 KO analysis with reference to Figure 8—figure supplement 5C

claim: Mice lacking the human mutations/deletions of the Nlg3 gene are useful animal models to study the mechanisms of ASD since they recapitulate most of behavioral deficits found in autistic children.
source: Mice carrying the human mutations/deletions of the Nlg3 gene are useful animal models to study the mechanisms of ASD since they recapitulate most of behavioral deficits found in autistic children.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about NLG3 KO mouse model

claim: Previous studies from NLG3 KO mice have highlighted alterations in synaptic signaling and network oscillations, associated with social deficits.
source: Previous studies from NLG3 KO mice have highlighted alterations in synaptic signaling and network oscillations, associated with social deficits (Földy et al., 2013; Modi et al., 2019; Tabuchi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Földy et al., 2013; Modi et al., 2019; Tabuchi et al., 2007

claim: NLGs are postsynaptic adhesion molecules that bind to their presynaptic partners neurexins to functionally couple the postsynaptic densities with the transmitter release machinery.
source: NLGs are postsynaptic adhesion molecules that bind to their presynaptic partners neurexins to functionally couple the postsynaptic densities with the transmitter release machinery, thus contributing to synapses organization and stabilization (Südhof, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Südhof, 2008

claim: Oscillatory activities, and in particular the gamma ones, depend on the synchronous firing of large neuronal ensembles of excitatory cells within and across brain regions, which are paced by GABAergic interneurons.
source: Oscillatory activities, and in particular the gamma ones, depend on the synchronous firing of large neuronal ensembles of excitatory cells within and across brain regions, which are paced by GABAergic interneurons (Gonzalez-Burgos and Lewis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonzalez-Burgos and Lewis, 2008

claim: GABAergic interneurons containing parvalbumin (PV+) and cholecystokinin (CCK+) are known to contribute to generate theta and gamma rhythms.
source: Therefore, the observed alterations in power may be due to a reduced GABA release from GABAergic interneurons such as those containing parvalbumin (PV+) and cholecystokinin (CCK+) known to contribute to generate theta and gamma rhythms (Klausberger et al., 2005; Tukker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klausberger et al., 2005; Tukker et al., 2007

claim: In NLG3 KO mice, there was a clear increase in GABA release from CCK+GABAergic interneurons into CA1 principal cells due to the impairment of tonic endocannabinoid signaling.
source: Interestingly, in a previous study from NLG3 KO mice (Földy et al., 2013), a clear increase in GABA release from CCK+GABAergic interneurons into CA1 principal cells was detected due to the impairment of tonic endocannabinoid signaling.
evidence: Supported by citation to Földy et al., 2013

claim: An impairment of GABAergic currents was reported in CA2 region of NLG3 KO mice.
source: Additionally, an impairment of GABAergic currents was also reported in CA2 region of NLG3 KO mice (Modi et al., 2019), an upstream region to CA1 (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Kohara et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Modi et al., 2019; Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Kohara et al., 2014

claim: The reduced oscillatory activity in NLG3 KO mice is probably mediated by the loss of GABAA-mediated neurotransmission in both CA1 and CA2 hippocampal regions.
source: Therefore, the reduced oscillatory activity reported here is probably mediated by the loss of GABAA-mediated neurotransmission in both CA1 and CA2 hippocampal regions.
evidence: Inference from previous findings about GABAergic impairments in NLG3 KO mice

claim: Loss of GABAA-mediated neurotransmission would cause an enhancement of network excitability with consequent excitatory/inhibitory unbalance, critical for controlling spike rate and information processing.
source: This would cause an enhancement of network excitability with consequent excitatory/inhibitory unbalance, critical for controlling spike rate and information processing.
evidence: Inference from proposed mechanism of reduced oscillatory activity

claim: The state space approach can be applied to study oscillations from multiple brain regions simultaneously and how one set of oscillations from one region influence the others.
source: (i) Assessment of inter-areal communication. The state space approach can be applied to study oscillations from multiple brain regions simultaneously and how one set of oscillations from one region influence the others (Gervasoni et al., 2004).
evidence: Proposed application with citation to Gervasoni et al., 2004

claim: The analytical framework can be applied to study alterations in the organization of brain-wide network oscillations as signatures or biomarkers in various neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Additionally, this analytical framework can be applied to study alterations in the organization of brain-wide network oscillations as signatures or biomarkers in various neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: Proposed application described in discussion

claim: Using network state space method will allow assessing how multiple brain regions, and their oscillations are simultaneously affected under pharmacological treatment.
source: (iii) Network assessment of novel therapeutics. Newly developed drugs are required to be extensively tested for their harmful side effects. Using network state space method will allow assessing how multiple brain regions, and their oscillations are simultaneously affected under pharmacological treatment.
evidence: Proposed application described in discussion

claim: Information from network state space analysis can be used to predict potential side effects and develop better therapeutics in drug development.
source: Additionally, this information can be used to predict potential side effects and develop better therapeutics in drug development.
evidence: Proposed application described in discussion
